question: Your similarity selector returns three examples that are rewordings of the same refund ticket. What is the problem and the fix?
options: No problem: more similar examples always help more
They spend tokens on one pattern and over-weight it; skip candidates too similar to an example already chosen
The embedding model is broken; switch providers
Lower k to one so there can be no duplicates
explanation: Deduplication against what is already selected keeps the budget for examples that add information and gives some diversity.

question: During an eval, accuracy is suspiciously high. Each eval item also exists in the example pool. What is happening?
options: The selector retrieves the item itself with its label, so the model copies the answer: exclude eval items from the pool
The model memorized the eval set during training
Dynamic selection always inflates accuracy by a fixed amount
Nothing: high accuracy proves the prompt is good
explanation: This is answer leakage. Keep eval items out of the pool (or exclude exact matches at selection time) so the score measures generalization.

question: Why place the most similar example last, right before the real input?
options: Providers only read the last example
Models tend to weigh content closest to the question more, so the most relevant pattern should be nearest
explanation: Position matters in prompts. Ordering is cheap to control and worth testing in your evals.

question: A long example scores second but does not fit the remaining token budget. A shorter example scores fifth. What should the selector do?
options: Stop selecting: the budget is exhausted
Exceed the budget for the high-scoring example
Truncate the long example to fit
Skip the long example and keep walking the ranking, taking the shorter one if it fits and passes the other filters
explanation: Skipping keeps the budget useful. Truncating an example corrupts the pattern you are showing, and exceeding the budget defeats its purpose.
